<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader||FUNCTION|323}}</noinclude>{{smaller block|We have seen above that all single valued doubly periodic meromorphic functions, with the same periods, are rational functions of two variables <math>s</math>, <math>z</math> connected by an equation of the form <math>s^2 = 4z^3 + \text{A}z + \text{B}</math>. Taking account of the relation connecting these variables <math>s</math>, <math>z</math> with the argument of the doubly periodic functions (which was above denoted by <math>z</math>), it can then easily be seen that the theorem now proved is a generalization of the theorem proved previously establishing for a doubly periodic function a definite ''order''. There exists a generalization of another theorem also proved above for doubly periodic functions, namely, that the sum of the values of the argument in one parallelogram of periods for which a doubly periodic function takes a given value is independent of that value; this generalization, known as Abel's Theorem, is given § 17 below.}}

§ 17. ''Integrals of Algebraic Functions''.—In treatises on Integral Calculus it is proved that if <math>\text{R}(z)</math> denote any rational function, an indefinite integral <math>\int \text{R}(z)dz</math> can be evaluated in terms of rational and logarithmic functions, including the inverse trigonometrical functions. In generalization of this it was long ago discovered that if <math>s^2 = az^2 + bz + c</math> and <math>\text{R}(s, z)</math> be any rational function of <math>s</math>, <math>z</math> any integral <math>\int \text{R}(s, z)\, dz</math> can be evaluated in terms of rational functions of <math>s</math>, <math>z</math> and logarithms of such functions; the simplest case is <math>\int s^{-1}dz</math> or <math>\int (az^2+bz+c)^{-\frac{1}{2}}dz</math>. More generally if <math>f(s, z) = 0</math> be such a relation connecting <math>s</math>, <math>z</math> that when <math>\theta</math> is an appropriate rational function of <math>s</math> and <math>z</math> both <math>s</math> and <math>z</math> are rationally expressible, in virtue of <math>f(s,z) = 0</math> in terms of <math>\theta</math>, the integral <math>\int \text{R}(s,z)dz</math> is reducible to a form <math>\int \text{H}(\theta)d\theta</math>, where <math>\text{H}(\theta)</math> is rational in <math>\theta</math>, and can therefore also be evaluated by rational functions and logarithms of rational functions of <math>s</math> and <math>z</math>. It was natural to inquire whether a similar theorem holds for integrals <math>\int \text{R}(s,z)dz</math> wherein <math>s^2</math> is a cubic polynomial in <math>z</math>. The answer is in the negative. For instance, no one of the three integrals
{{block center|<math>\int \frac{dz}{s},\ \int \frac{zdz}{s},\ \int \frac{dz}{(z-c)s}</math>}}
can be expressed by rational and logarithms of rational functions of <math>s</math> and <math>z</math>; but it can be shown that every integral <math>\int \text{R}(s,z)dz</math> can be expressed by means of integrals of these three types together with rational and logarithms of rational functions of <math>s</math> and <math>z</math> (see below under § 20, ''Elliptic Integrals''). A similar theorem is true when <math>s^2 =</math> quartic polynomial in <math>z</math>; in fact when <math>s^2 = \text{A}(z-a)(z-b)(z-c)(z-d)</math>, putting <math>y = s(z-a)^{-2}</math>, <math>x = (z-a)^{-1}</math>, we obtain <math>y^2 =</math> cubic polynomial in <math>x</math>. Much less is the theorem true when the fundamental relation <math>f(s,z) = 0</math> is of more general type. There exists then, however, a very general theorem, known as ''Abel's Theorem'', which may be enunciated as follows: Beside the rational function <math>\text{R}(s, z)</math> occurring in the integral <math>\int \text{R}(s,z)dz</math>, consider another rational function <math>\text{H}(s,z)</math>; let <math>(a_1), \dots (a_m)</math> denote the places of the construct associated with the fundamental equation <math>f(s, z) = 0</math>, for which <math>\text{H}(s,z)</math> is equal to one value A, each taken with its proper multiplicity, and let <math>(b_1), \dots (b_m)</math> denote the places for which <math>\text{H}(s,z) = \text{B}</math>, where B is another value; then the sum of the <math>m</math> integrals <math>\int_{(a_i)}^{(b_i)} \text{R}(s,z)\,dz</math> is equal to the sum of the coefficients of <math>t^{-1}</math> in the expansions of the function
{{block center|<math>\text{R}(s,z)\frac{dz}{dt}\lambda\left(\frac{\text{H}(s,z)-\text{B}}{\text{H}(s,z)-\text{A}}\right)</math>,}}
where <math>\lambda</math> denotes the generalized logarithmic function, at the various places where the expansion of <math>\text{R}(s,z)dz/dt</math> contains negative powers of <math>t</math>. This fact may be obtained at once from the equation
{{block center|<math>\left[\frac{1}{\text{H}(s,z)-\mu}\text{R}(s,z)\frac{dz}{dt}\right]_{t^{-1}}=0</math>,}}
wherein <math>\mu</math> is a constant. (For illustrations see below, under § 20, ''Elliptic Integrals.'')

§ 18. ''Indeterminateness of Algebraic Integrals.''—The theorem that the integral <math>\int_a^z f(z)\,dz</math> is independent of the path from <math>a</math> to <math>z</math>, holds only on the hypothesis that any two such paths are equivalent, that is, taken together from the complete boundary of a region of the plane within which <math>f(z)</math> is finite and single valued, besides being differentiable. Suppose that these conditions fail only at a finite number of isolated points in the finite part of the plane. Then any path from <math>a</math> to <math>z</math> is equivalent, in the sense explained, to any other path together with closed paths beginning and ending at the arbitrary point <math>a</math> each enclosing one or more of the exceptional points, these closed paths being chosen, when <math>f(z)</math> is not a single valued function, so that the final value of <math>f(z)</math> at <math>a</math> is equal to its initial value. It is necessary for the statement that this condition may be capable of being satisfied.

{{smaller block|For instance, the integral <math>\int_1^z z^{-1}dz</math> is liable to an additive indeterminateness equal to the value obtained by a closed path about <math>z=0</math>, which is equal to <math>2\pi i</math>; if we put <math>u=\int_1^z z^{-1}dz</math> and consider <math>z</math> as a function of <math>u</math>, then we must regard this function as unaffected by the addition of <math>2\pi i</math> to its argument <math>u</math>; we know in fact that <math>z=\text{exp}\,(u)</math> and is a single valued function of <math>u</math>, with the period <math>2\pi i</math>. Or again the integral <math>\int_0^z (1+z^2)^{-1}dz</math> is liable to an additive indeterminateness equal to the value obtained by a closed path about either of the points <math>z=\pm i</math>; thus if we put <math>u=\int_0^z (1+z^2)^{-1}dz</math>, the function <math>z</math> of <math>u</math> is periodic with period <math>\pi</math>, this being the function <math>\text{tan}\,(u)</math>. Next we take the integral <math>u=\int_{(0)}^{(z)} (1-z^2)^{-\frac{1}{2}}dz</math>, agreeing that the upper and lower limits refer not only to definite values of <math>z</math>, but to definite values of <math>z</math> each associated with a definite determination}} of the sign of the associated radical <math>(1-z^2)^{-\frac{1}{2}}</math>. We suppose <math>1+z</math>, <math>1-z</math> each to have phase zero for <math>z=0</math>; then a single closed circuit of <math>z=-1</math> will lead back to <math>z=0</math> with <math>(1-z^2)^{\frac{1}{2}}=-1</math>; the additive indeterminateness of the integral, obtained by a closed path which restores the initial value of the subject of integration, may be obtained by a closed circuit containing both the points <math>\pm 1</math> in its interior; this gives, since the integral taken about a vanishing circle whose centre is either of the points <math>z=\pm 1</math> has ultimately the value zero, the sum
{{block center|<math>\int_0^{-1}\frac{dz}{(1-z^2)^{\frac{1}{2}}}+\int_{-1}^0\frac{dz}{-(1-z^2)^{\frac{1}{2}}}+\int_0^1\frac{dz}{-(1-z^2)^{\frac{1}{2}}}+\int_1^0\frac{dz}{(1-z^2)^{\frac{1}{2}}},</math>}}
where, in each case, <math>(1-z^2)^{\frac{1}{2}}</math> is real and positive; that is, it gives
{{block center|<math>-4\int_0^1\frac{dz}{(1-z^2)^{\frac{1}{2}}}</math>}}
or <math>2\pi</math>. Thus the additive indeterminateness of the integral is of the form <math>2k\pi</math>, where <math>k</math> is an integer, and the function <math>z</math> of <math>u</math>, which is <math>\sin(u)</math>, has <math>2\pi</math> for period. Take now the case
{{block center|<math>u=\int_{(z_0)}^{(z)}\frac{dz}{\sqrt{\{(z-a)(z-b)(z-c)(z-d)\}}},</math>}}
adopting a definite determination for the phase of each of the factors <math>z-a</math>, <math>z-b</math>, <math>z-c</math>, <math>z-d</math> at the arbitrary point <math>z_0</math>, and supposing the upper limit to refer, not only to a definite value of <math>z</math>, but also to a definite determination of the radical under the sign of integration. From <math>z_0</math> describe a closed loop about the point <math>z=a</math>, consisting, suppose, of a straight path from <math>z_0</math> to <math>a</math>, followed by a vanishing circle whose centre is at <math>a</math>, completed by the straight path from <math>a</math> to <math>z_0</math>. Let similar loops be imagined for each of the points <math>b</math>, <math>c</math>, <math>d</math>, no two of these having a point in common. Let <math>\text{A}</math> denote the value obtained by the positive circuit of the first loop; this will be in fact equal to twice the integral taken from <math>z_0</math> along the straight path to <math>a</math>; for the contribution due to the vanishing circle is ultimately zero, and the effect of the circuit of this circle is to change the sign of the subject of integration. After the circuit about <math>a</math>, we arrive back at <math>z_0</math> with the subject of integration changed in sign; let <math>\text{B}</math>, <math>\text{C}</math>, <math>\text{D}</math> denote the values of the integral taken by the loops enclosing respectively <math>b</math>, <math>c</math> and <math>d</math> when in each case the initial determination of the subject of integration is that adopted in calculating <math>\text{A}</math>.
